name: Alcove-Thalassic
geological_features: Sheltered coastal alcove formations in volcanic rock
specific_features: Bioluminescent tidal pools that synchronize their light displays
description: Alcove-Thalassic is an oceanic world graced with thousands of volcanic island chains, their coastlines carved into sheltered alcoves and sea caves by millennia of wave action. The islands rise steeply from warm, shallow seas rich with coral reef analogues, their dark basalt shores honeycomed with tidal caves that flood and drain with metronomic regularity. The deeper waters between island chains are clear to remarkable depths, revealing submarine volcanic landscapes of rugged beauty.

The atmosphere is warm, salt-laden, and breathable, carrying the constant sound of waves and the calls of aerial fauna that nest in the cliff alcoves. At night, the tidal pools that fill the coastal alcoves produce synchronized bioluminescent displays, waves of blue-green light that pulse outward from individual pools and align with neighboring pools in patterns spanning entire island coastlines. The effect is mesmerizing, as though the ocean itself is signaling.

The synchronized bioluminescence has been traced to a colonial organism that inhabits the tidal pools, a cnidarian analogue whose light production is triggered by pressure waves in the water. As tides pulse through the alcove networks, the organisms respond in sequence, creating the appearance of coordinated display. Whether this serves a biological purpose or is merely an emergent property of the tidal rhythm remains debated among marine biologists.

Alcove-Thalassic's medicinal compounds, particularly those derived from its coral analogues, have shown promise in treating inflammatory and autoimmune conditions. The sheltered alcoves provide natural harbor sites for research stations, and several are already operational. The planet has been proposed as a marine biology preserve, but its accessibility and mild conditions have also attracted colonial interest. Balancing research, preservation, and settlement is the ongoing challenge.
